paras: The threatened lynching of Solomon Marable, Pokey Barnes and Mary Abernathy was a reported threat of mob violence against three Black prisoners charged with the murder of Lucy Jane Pollard in Lunenburg County, Virginia, in June and July 1895. The prisoners were tried at Lunenburg Courthouse under the guard of three militia companies and sentenced to hang; none was harmed by a crowd. In August, Richmond critics called the convictions verdicts dictated by a mob, and Lunenburg citizens answered that the danger had been invented.

Mrs. Lucy J. Pollard was killed in her yard near the Charlotte County line on June 14, 1895. Marable was captured at Five Forks in Mecklenburg County and, by the citizens' account, confessed and named Abernathy and Barnes as his accomplices; a fourth woman, Mary Barnes, was later charged as an accessory.

A Fort Mitchell resident wrote that after the capture the guards "became frightened and carried the prisoners to jail during the night" because of a gathering that, he said, came only to learn what had been decided. On June 19 the three were sent to the Petersburg jail; a later petition for one of the women said the people of the county had been so threatening that the sheriff moved her "stealthily in the night-time." According to the petition, the sheriff, prosecutor and judge then asked the governor for troops, and on July 11 Sheriff M. C. Cardozo ordered Major J. H. Derbyshire to keep the prisoners from being taken from his custody.

Companies A and B of the First Regiment Virginia Volunteers brought the prisoners to Lunenburg Courthouse on July 12 and guarded the jail and courtroom. Derbyshire reported that he became "more and more convinced that additional troops were necessary," and Company D arrived on July 17. The defendants had no counsel apart from a lawyer who moved for a change of venue and withdrew when it was overruled. The trials ended on July 20 with death sentences for the three and, by a critic's account, ten years for the fourth woman, and the militia took the condemned to the Richmond jail the next day.

The Richmond lawyers George D. Wise and H. W. Flournoy took up the women's cases and sought a new trial. A Topeka paper reported that most of the militiamen believed the women innocent and that "Editor John Mitchell of the Richmond Planet has interested himself in behalf of the women."
Lunenburg residents met at the courthouse in late July and on August 6, when about fifty attended, and adopted resolutions against the Richmond Times, the military and Captain F. W. Cunningham.

Coverage centered on the two Richmond dailies, from early August into September. The Times held that the women were sentenced "in obedience to the predetermination of a mob" and had been kept in Petersburg "to save them from the fury of the mob," while calling Marable a "stupid, brutal, Congo negro." The Dispatch ran both a letter calling the convictions "lynchings according to law" and a Lunenburg reply, and the county meeting praised it as "a friend of our people."

The Lunenburg resolutions declared that the county had never had a lynching, yet warned that "we must and will protect our wives and daughters without law" if convicted criminals went free. Outside Virginia, short items on the new-trial effort ran in The Afro-American and the Weekly Call of Topeka, which described the victim as "a white woman."

The letter-writer Saunders, the Times and the petition said crowds threatened the prisoners from arrest through trial, Saunders citing dispatches stating "that all three would be lynched" if the second woman were acquitted. The Fort Mitchell writer called such reports "grossly exaggerated," and a Lunenburg writer said fewer than thirty white citizens attended the trials at any one time and that "The powerful mob we have heard so much about was only in imagination." Ex-sheriff J. W. Ellis certified that the danger had passed once the prisoners reached Petersburg. The denials came from residents of the county whose conduct was in question, the accounts of danger from the militia commander, the defense and Richmond critics.

bases: Militia guarded three Black prisoners accused of murder because officials and critics said a mob threatened to lynch them (A5, A10, A16); no one was killed, and local residents denied the threat (A1, A14).

No one was killed: the three prisoners were tried, sentenced and returned to jail under militia guard (A5). The reported threat was framed as punishment for the Pollard murder (A10, A13), but its existence and the size of any crowd are disputed (A1, A14).

The militia commander's report, a critic's letter, Times editorials and the defendant's petition describe danger of mob violence (A5, A10, A13, A16), while a Fort Mitchell resident, Lunenburg resolutions and an ex-sheriff deny any real danger (A1, A9, A14).

accounts.label: Militia commander's report
accounts.gist: Derbyshire guarded the prisoners at the sheriff's order and called for a third company after becoming convinced more troops were needed.

accounts.label: Critic's letter (Saunders)
accounts.gist: Excitement forced the prisoners to Petersburg and militia guarded them from mob violence; dispatches said all three would be lynched if one woman were acquitted.

accounts.label: Defendant's petition
accounts.gist: Threatening conduct forced the sheriff to remove the prisoners by night, and officials sought troops against mob violence.

accounts.label: Lunenburg residents
accounts.gist: There was no real danger after the prisoners were jailed; the gathering after capture was misunderstood and the troops were unnecessary.

framing.detail: The Richmond Times said the women were condemned 'in obedience to the predetermination of a mob' while describing the accused in demeaning racial terms.
The Richmond Dispatch ran the 'lynchings according to law' letter and the militia report alongside Lunenburg denials, and was praised by the county meeting.
Lunenburg resolutions denied the threat and warned residents would protect 'wives and daughters without law'.
Out-of-state items in The Afro-American and The Weekly Call reported the new-trial effort and doubts of the women's guilt.
